goldenPoints: Tuning fork for clinical testing is 512 Hz; Rinne negative means conductive loss.
Scanty, foul, blood-stained discharge = cholesteatoma = unsafe CSOM = mastoid surgery.
Little's area (Kiesselbach plexus) on the anteroinferior septum is the commonest epistaxis site.
Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor of the vocal cords.
External laryngeal nerve injury after thyroid surgery = singer cannot raise pitch.
Type B flat tympanogram = middle-ear effusion; in an adult think nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
Beta-2 transferrin is the most specific confirmation of CSF rhinorrhoea.
Meniere's disease is endolymphatic hydrops: vertigo, fluctuating SNHL, tinnitus, fullness.
JNA occurs in adolescent boys — diagnose on imaging, never biopsy.
Commonest cause of stridor in a newborn/infant is laryngomalacia.
intro: ENT carries 15 questions in every FMGE paper. The stems repeat around hearing tests and tympanometry, safe vs unsafe CSOM, Meniere's disease, Little's area, vocal cord palsy and classic syndromes like Gradenigo and Samter. Revise these 12 topics and you cover most of what the last five years actually asked.
subject: ENT
tagline: Tuning forks, CSOM, vertigo, epistaxis and vocal-cord palsy — ENT marks come from a small set of repeat patterns.

topics.askedAs: Rinne/Weber interpretation in a clinical stem
topics.oneLiner: Rinne negative + Weber to same ear = conductive loss in that ear.
points: Tuning fork used for routine testing: 512 Hz
Rinne positive (AC > BC) = normal ear or sensorineural loss
Rinne negative (BC > AC) = conductive hearing loss
Weber lateralises to the worse ear in conductive loss, to the better ear in sensorineural loss
Absolute bone conduction (ABC) is reduced only in sensorineural loss
Schwabach: patient's BC compared with examiner's — shortened in SNHL, lengthened in CHL
Stapedial reflex arc: afferent CN VIII, efferent CN VII (stapedius)
BERA is an objective test — used in infants, malingerers and retrocochlear lesions
Otoacoustic emissions (OAE) is the most common newborn hearing screening test
topics.title: Tuning Fork Tests & Hearing Assessment
topics.trap: In severe unilateral SNHL, a false Rinne negative appears because bone conduction is heard by the opposite cochlea.

topics.askedAs: Type B / As / Ad curve — name the condition
topics.oneLiner: Flat type B = fluid; shallow As = otosclerosis; Carhart notch at 2 kHz confirms it.
points: Type A: normal middle ear pressure and compliance
Type As (shallow peak at 0 daPa): otosclerosis / stiff ossicular chain
Type Ad (deep, high peak): ossicular discontinuity
Type B (flat curve): fluid in middle ear — otitis media with effusion, glue ear
Type C (peak at negative pressure): Eustachian tube dysfunction, retracted drum
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma classically presents with unilateral serous otitis media (type B) in an adult
Carhart notch: dip at 2000 Hz in bone conduction — signature of otosclerosis
Meniere's disease: low-frequency sensorineural loss on audiogram
Presbyacusis: bilateral high-frequency SNHL in the elderly with poor speech discrimination
topics.title: Tympanometry & Audiogram Patterns
topics.trap: Type B also occurs with a perforated drum with discharge — read the stem for effusion clues before answering glue ear.

topics.askedAs: Foul scanty discharge + complication = atticoantral disease
topics.oneLiner: Scanty + foul + blood-stained = cholesteatoma = unsafe ear = surgery.
points: Tubotympanic (safe) type: central perforation, mucoid odourless discharge, no cholesteatoma
Atticoantral (unsafe) type: marginal/attic perforation with cholesteatoma
Cholesteatoma: scanty, foul-smelling, blood-stained discharge that never fully clears
Most common complication overall: mastoiditis
Most common intracranial complication: meningitis; most common extracranial: mastoid abscess
Brain abscess from CSOM most often involves the temporal lobe (then cerebellum)
Labyrinthine fistula most commonly erodes the lateral semicircular canal
Gradenigo syndrome: retro-orbital pain (CN V), diplopia (CN VI) + otorrhoea — petrous apicitis
Modified radical mastoidectomy is the treatment of choice for cholesteatoma
topics.title: CSOM — Safe vs Unsafe Ear
topics.trap: Profuse mucoid discharge points to the SAFE ear; examiners swap 'scanty' and 'profuse' to trap you.

topics.askedAs: Pregnant woman with hearing loss / child with dull drum
topics.oneLiner: Young woman, worse hearing in pregnancy, Schwartz sign = otosclerosis; stapedotomy cures.
points: Otosclerosis: fixation of stapes footplate; commoner in women, worsens in pregnancy
Schwartz sign: flamingo-pink blush of the promontory seen through the drum
Paracusis Willisii: patient hears better in noisy surroundings
Treatment of choice for otosclerosis: stapedectomy / stapedotomy
Glue ear (OME): dull, retracted drum with fluid level/air bubbles; type B tympanogram
Adenoid hypertrophy is the commonest cause of OME in children; high-arched palate is a clue
Symptomatic adenoid hypertrophy: adenoidectomy ± grommet (ventilation tube)
Acute otitis media: bulging red drum, severe pain; most common organism Streptococcus pneumoniae
Insect in the ear: kill it first with oil/water instillation, then remove
topics.title: Otosclerosis, Glue Ear & Otitis Media
topics.trap: Otosclerosis causes conductive loss, not sensorineural — the cochlea is normal early on.

topics.oneLiner: Hydrops gives vertigo + fullness + roaring tinnitus; Dix–Hallpike is for BPPV, not Meniere's.
points: Meniere's disease = endolymphatic hydrops of the inner ear
Classic tetrad: episodic vertigo, fluctuating SNHL, tinnitus, aural fullness
Vertigo lasts 20 minutes to 12 hours; low-frequency roaring tinnitus
Tullio phenomenon: vertigo induced by loud sound
NOT a feature: loss of consciousness / post-aural pain — pick the odd one out carefully
Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre diagnoses BPPV — posterior canal is the commonest site
BPPV is treated by the Epley canalith repositioning manoeuvre
Vestibular neuronitis: vertigo after viral illness, hearing normal
Acoustic neuroma: unilateral SNHL with poor speech discrimination, tinnitus; arises from vestibular division of CN VIII
topics.title: Meniere's Disease & Vertigo
topics.trap: Meniere's vertigo is episodic with ear symptoms; continuous vertigo without ear symptoms points elsewhere.

topics.askedAs: Diabetic with severe ear pain + granulations
topics.oneLiner: Diabetic + Pseudomonas + skull-base granulations = malignant otitis externa.
points: Malignant (necrotising) otitis externa: elderly diabetic, severe otalgia, granulations in canal floor
Causative organism: Pseudomonas aeruginosa in most cases
It is an osteomyelitis of the skull base — can involve CN VII, then IX–XII
Ramsay Hunt syndrome: herpes zoster oticus — vesicles in the ear canal + LMN facial palsy
Bell palsy: idiopathic LMN facial palsy; whole face including forehead involved
Frey syndrome: gustatory sweating after parotidectomy — auriculotemporal nerve fibres misdirected
Referred otalgia after tonsillectomy travels via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Syncopal attack during ear syringing: stimulation of the vagus nerve (Arnold's branch)
topics.title: Malignant Otitis Externa & Ramsay Hunt
topics.trap: Facial palsy with forehead sparing is UMN (stroke); Bell/Ramsay Hunt involve the forehead — LMN.

topics.askedAs: Site of bleeding / Kiesselbach plexus stem
topics.oneLiner: Anterior septum, Little's area, Kiesselbach plexus — the most tested address in ENT.
points: Little's area lies on the anteroinferior nasal septum — commonest site of epistaxis
Kiesselbach plexus: anastomosis of septal branches in Little's area
Woodruff plexus (posterior, venous) causes posterior epistaxis in elderly hypertensives
Retrocolumellar vein is the usual source of bleeding in children
First aid: sit up, lean forward, pinch the soft nose (Trotter's method)
Anterior bleed uncontrolled → anterior nasal packing; posterior bleed → posterior pack / Foley catheter
Ligation options: sphenopalatine artery (endoscopic), anterior ethmoidal, external carotid, maxillary
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler–Weber–Rendu): recurrent epistaxis + telangiectasia
Long-term topical decongestant abuse causes rhinitis medicamentosa with rebound congestion
topics.title: Epistaxis & Little's Area
topics.trap: Posterior epistaxis is venous (Woodruff) in the elderly; don't label every bleed arterial.

topics.askedAs: Adolescent boy with epistaxis + posterior choanal mass
topics.oneLiner: Teenage boy + epistaxis + choanal mass = JNA — image it, never biopsy it.
points: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma: adolescent males only, recurrent severe epistaxis
JNA arises from the sphenopalatine foramen area; staged by Radkowski system
Never biopsy a suspected JNA — it bleeds torrentially; diagnose on imaging, treat by excision
Inverted papilloma: benign but locally aggressive, recurs, can turn malignant (squamous cell carcinoma)
Antrochoanal polyp: single, arises from maxillary antrum, exits via choana; seen in the young
Ethmoidal polyps: multiple, bilateral, allergic; Samter triad = polyps + asthma + aspirin sensitivity
Mucormycosis: diabetic/immunosuppressed, black necrotic eschar, invades vessels, erodes palate and orbit
Rhinoscleroma: Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis; Mikulicz cells and Russell bodies
Atrophic rhinitis (ozaena): foul greenish crusts, anosmia, roomy nasal cavity; Klebsiella ozaenae
topics.title: Nasal Masses: JNA, Inverted Papilloma, Polyps, Mucormycosis
topics.trap: Antrochoanal polyp is single and unilateral; ethmoidal polyps are multiple and bilateral.

topics.askedAs: Posterior triangle nodes + unilateral ear effusion
topics.oneLiner: Fossa of Rosenmüller + EBV + radiotherapy; beta-2 transferrin proves CSF.
points: Commonest site of nasopharyngeal carcinoma: fossa of Rosenmüller
NPC is associated with Epstein–Barr virus; common in South-East Asia / Nagaland belt stems
Presents with posterior triangle cervical nodes, unilateral serous otitis media, epistaxis, CN palsies
Trotter triad in NPC: conductive deafness, palatal immobility, trigeminal neuralgia
Treatment of choice for NPC: radiotherapy (tumour is radiosensitive)
CSF rhinorrhoea: clear watery discharge, salty taste, increases on bending/straining
Beta-2 transferrin is the most specific test confirming CSF in nasal discharge
Commonest cause of CSF rhinorrhoea: trauma (cribriform plate fracture → anosmia too)
Initial management of traumatic CSF leak: conservative — head elevation, avoid straining; most stop spontaneously
topics.title: Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma & CSF Rhinorrhoea
topics.trap: Glucose oxidase strips are unreliable for CSF — beta-2 transferrin is the answer examiners want.

topics.askedAs: Hoarseness after thyroid surgery / singer losing high notes
topics.oneLiner: PCA abducts alone; recurrent laryngeal does everything except cricothyroid.
points: Posterior cricoarytenoid is the ONLY abductor of the vocal cords
All intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve except cricothyroid
Cricothyroid is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve — the pitch/tension nerve
Singer who cannot hit high notes after thyroid surgery: external laryngeal nerve injury
Internal laryngeal nerve injury: loss of cough reflex above the cords → aspiration risk
Commonest cause of unilateral vocal cord palsy: malignant tumours (lung apex, thyroid, oesophagus)
Bilateral abductor palsy: cords sit in median position → stridor, airway emergency, needs tracheostomy
Unilateral palsy: cord in paramedian position, hoarseness with a breathy voice
Killian dehiscence: gap between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus — site of Zenker diverticulum
topics.title: Larynx: Vocal Cord Palsy & Nerves
topics.trap: Bilateral palsy threatens the AIRWAY (cords together); unilateral palsy mainly spoils the voice.

topics.askedAs: Teacher/singer with hoarseness — pick the lesion
topics.oneLiner: Nodules are bilateral in voice abusers; laryngomalacia is the infant stridor answer.
points: Vocal nodules: bilateral, at junction of anterior 1/3 and posterior 2/3 of cords — singers and teachers
Vocal polyp: usually unilateral, follows voice abuse or a single shouting episode
Reinke oedema: diffuse swelling of Reinke space in smokers; husky, low-pitched voice
Laryngomalacia: commonest cause of stridor in infants; omega-shaped epiglottis; self-limiting
Laryngeal cancer T1b: tumour involving BOTH vocal cords with normal mobility
Glottis is the commonest subsite of laryngeal carcinoma; hoarseness is its earliest symptom
HPV is most strongly linked to oropharyngeal (tonsil/base of tongue) squamous carcinoma
Contact ulcer: posterior cord, from acid reflux and throat clearing
Rhinolalia clausa (closed nasality) is NOT seen in cleft palate — that gives open nasality (aperta)
topics.title: Laryngeal & Voice Disorders
topics.trap: Cleft palate causes rhinolalia APERTA (open), never clausa — a favourite 'not seen in' stem.

topics.askedAs: Trismus + abscess / foreign body level stem
topics.oneLiner: Trismus near a throat abscess = medial pterygoid spasm; cricopharyngeus traps the fish bone.
points: Parapharyngeal abscess: trismus from spasm of the medial pterygoid muscle
Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy): uvula pushed to opposite side, hot-potato voice, trismus
Crypta magna is the remnant of the second pharyngeal pouch (in the tonsil)
Ludwig angina: cellulitis of the submandibular space, usually dental in origin — airway first
Commonest site of fish-bone impaction: the tonsil; oesophageal narrowing at cricopharyngeus (~15 cm from incisors) is the commonest oesophageal site
Aortic arch crossing is at ~25 cm from incisors; cardia at ~40 cm
Laryngocele: trumpet players / glass blowers; neck swelling that gurgles on compression
Blow-out fracture of orbit floor: enophthalmos, diplopia, infraorbital anaesthesia after a ball injury
Bleeding from the ear after head injury: HRCT temporal bone is the investigation of choice
topics.title: Deep Neck Spaces, Tonsils & Obstructions
topics.trap: Quinsy pushes the uvula AWAY from the affected side — stems test the direction.
